title: 2 · Rolling-origin backtest
text: The question of the plan is not “can I run a TSFM” but when it beats a specialist and when it loses, said with the coverage of its intervals and not only its mean MASE. Every step below answers part of that.

title: 2 · Rolling-origin backtest
section: 1. Look at the series before modelling it
text:
1. Look at the series before modelling it







NoteIntuition



National load is a sum of millions of consumers. It is smooth from hour to hour, it repeats every day and every week, and in France it follows the temperature in winter (electric heating). A good forecaster reads three things: the current level, the daily shape and the weekly shape.










WarningWatch out



Raw ENTSO-E data contain one hour at 158 GW, against a national record of about 102 GW, and 9 gaps. A single such value in a target window would dominate a mean error. Values outside [20, 110] GW are set to missing. Gaps are filled for inputs only, and an imputed hour is never scored.

title: 2 · Rolling-origin backtest
text:
2. Choose the baselines honestly

The plan’s naive repeats yesterday, so it forecasts Monday with Sunday. I expected it to be a strawman. The measurement says it beats the weekly naive on five weekdays out of seven, so both stay. The real specialist is MSTL, the only statistical model here that carries both cycles.

title: 2 · Rolling-origin backtest
section: 3. The protocol: what each model may read
text:
3. The protocol: what each model may read







NoteExample



At the origin 2019-03-12 00:00 UTC, AutoETS is refitted on the 672 hours that end at 2019-03-11 23:00. Chronos-Bolt reads the 2048 hours that end at the same hour and is not refitted. Both forecast 2019-03-12 00:00 to 23:00, and the next day the origin moves by 24 hours. tests/test_backtest.py corrupts every value after an origin and checks that its forecast does not move.


The protocol (origins, windows, metrics, verdict rule) was committed before the first forecast. Rule: a challenger beats the reference on a regime if the 95% block-bootstrap CI of its MASE ratio is below 1. It is “deployable as-is” if its 90% coverage is in [0.85, 0.95].

sMAPE is utilsforecast’s |e|/(|y|+|f|), half the textbook one. width90 is a fraction of the load. Winkler90 and SQL (scaled quantile loss over 0.1-0.9) are divided by the MASE scale.







WarningWatch out: the reference forecasts a flat line



AutoETS chooses its model by AICc, a one-step likelihood. On smooth hourly data, the level-only model wins at 572 of 608 origins and forecasts 24 times the last value. “Chronos beats AutoETS by a factor 4” is true but says little. A reference with forced seasonality (ETS Z,Z,A) was added after seeing this and is labelled as a deviation. Against it, the factor is 2.5.








WarningWatch out: a flat line can be perfectly calibrated



The flat AutoETS covers 0.899 of hours with its 90% interval, almost exactly nominal, because the interval is 45% of the load wide. Coverage alone rewards a useless interval. The Winkler score, which charges the width, ranks it last.

title: 2 · Rolling-origin backtest
section: 5. Where does the “90%” interval come from?
text:
5. Where does the “90%” interval come from?







ImportantThe trap of the plan, measured



Chronos-Bolt was trained on 9 quantiles, 0.1 to 0.9. Asked for 0.05 and 0.95, it returns its 0.1 and 0.9: its 90% interval is its 80% interval. In the table, cov80 = cov90 = 0.858. It lands inside the band only because its 80% interval over-covers, and the CI of that coverage (0.833-0.884) crosses the band’s edge. The pre-registered rule says WINS; the honest reading is “calibrated by accident”. A split-conformal repair keeps its median and rebuilds the intervals from its own past errors: 0.902.

TipTakeaway: the one sentence of the plan



On French hourly load in 2019, Chronos-Bolt base beats AutoETS at every horizon step and on every ordinary day type (MASE ratio 0.24, or 0.40 against a seasonal ETS), with a 90% coverage of 0.86. That interval is its 80% one by construction, and it under-covers on h 13-18 (0.79). On public holidays it is no better than the seasonal ETS and its interval covers 37% of the hours: zero-shot, it does not know the calendar.


The specialists fail on holidays too, but a specialist can be given a holiday flag, while a zero-shot univariate TSFM cannot be told. The conformal repair does not save holidays (0.40), because it calibrates on average over the previous 56 days, not conditionally on a rare day.

title: 2 · Rolling-origin backtest
section: 7. Six origins, as in the plan?
text:
7. Six origins, as in the plan?

With 6 origins drawn at random, the comparison against the seasonal ETS is right 99.8% of the time, since the gap is a factor 2.5. Against MSTL, the close contest, a quarter of the draws reverse it. The minimum of the plan detects large gaps and cannot settle close ones.

text:
8. Stress and sensitivity








NoteExploratory, not pre-registered



With one week of context, Bolt base (0.452) already beats MSTL fitted on eight weeks (0.479). That is the cold-start argument the router of block 3 tests across 50 series. The best context on 2019 (1024 h) is not adopted, because it was found on the test year.

title: 4 · Reading: the MASE
text:
NoteIntuition



An error of 1,000 MW is large for Belgium and small for Germany. A percentage fixes that, but it breaks near zero. The MASE divides the error by the error a naive method made on the same series in the past. It answers “how much better than doing nothing clever?”, in a unit that is the same for every series.
\[
\text{MASE} = \frac{\frac{1}{h}\sum_{j=1}^{h} |y_{T+j} - \hat y_{T+j}|}{\frac{1}{T-m}\sum_{t=m+1}^{T} |y_t - y_{t-m}|}
\]
The 2006 paper defines it with m = 1 (one-step naive). The seasonal version with lag m is FPP3 section 5.8. This study uses m = 24.

title: 4 · Reading: the MASE
text: Why not MAPE

title: 4 · Reading: the MASE
text:
Why not sMAPE either







WarningWatch out



For y = 100 and an error of 60, sMAPE gives 86% if the forecast is low and 46% if it is high. A model that over-forecasts looks better. utilsforecast’s smape is moreover half the textbook formula.

title: 4 · Reading: the MASE
text: What scale-free buys

title: 4 · Reading: the MASE
text:
The scale is a choice







TipTakeaway



With m = 24, SeasonalNaive(24) scores 1.01: out of sample it repeats the method that defines the scale. With m = 1, the same forecasts score 1.72. “MASE below 1” only means something once m and the horizon are stated.

title: 3 · The Complexity Router, out of sample
text:
NoteIntuition



A router is a bet: for some series the shared zero-shot model is good enough, or better, and a dedicated model is a waste. For others, the dedicated model is worth its upkeep. The router is right if (a) such series exist and (b) it can recognise them before seeing the test period.

title: 3 · The Complexity Router, out of sample
text:
What a cost-aware router buys







ImportantAn oracle is not a policy



The red curve sorts units by their realised gain: it is the best any router could do, and it needs the answer. The paper’s headline (0.970, a 70% cost cut) is such a curve. Out of sample, our stump stays within 0.015 MASE of it between 25% and 100% of TSFM calls. The paper’s rule sits above the random line.


And the cost itself: Chronos-2 takes about 95 ms per series on 4 CPU threads, or about 5 ms in a GPU batch. An MSTL refit takes 183 ms on one core. The paper’s assumed 1000x ratio describes a specialist that only predicts. A specialist that refits every day costs as much as the TSFM.

title: 3 · The Complexity Router, out of sample
text:
The router drifts







TipTakeaway



Re-evaluated every 5 days on the trailing 4 weeks, a cost-aware rule on acf_24 moves 40 of 50 series and swings the TSFM share from 12% to 78%. A ±0.05 hysteresis band cuts the flips from 323 to 78. A router is a model: it needs its own monitoring, its own owner and versioned thresholds.

WarningWatch out: an oracle is not a policy



Sorting series by their realised FM advantage and routing the best ones first gives the best possible curve, but it needs the test set’s answer. The deployed rule, with thresholds learned on a calibration split, matches the FM’s accuracy and saves a third of its calls. That is still useful, and much less than “70%”. NoteContamination



Chronos-2’s training list has no ENTSO-E or OPSD data. Chronos-Bolt’s corpus is not itemised. If it reuses the Chronos corpus, it contains Spanish national load 2015-2018, built from ENTSO-E: the same years and provider, another country. No overlap with French load is documented. All three weights are Apache-2.0; IBM’s TTM-r3 is non-commercial (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0).

title: When does a zero-shot TSFM beat a refitted specialist?
text: The plan of the week (a French brief, ISO week 25 of 2026) asks one question: when does a time series foundation model beat a supervised specialist, and when does it lose? And how do we turn that decision into a production component? It asks for the answer in one sentence, backed by interval coverage and not only by a mean error.

title: When does a zero-shot TSFM beat a refitted specialist?
text:
The answers






TipBlock 2, the sentence the plan asks for



On French hourly load in 2019, Chronos-Bolt base beats AutoETS at every horizon step and on every ordinary day type (MASE ratio 0.24, or 0.40 against an ETS with forced seasonality), with a 90% coverage of 0.86. That interval is its 80% one by construction. It under-covers on h 13-18 (0.79). On public holidays it is no better than the seasonal ETS and covers 37% of hours: zero-shot, it does not know the calendar. Told the calendar (a holiday flag as a known covariate, exploratory), Chronos-2 halves its holiday error and its yearly 90% coverage becomes 0.899.








TipBlock 3, the router



On 50 load series, Chronos-2 wins on all 200 (series, history) units, and most in cold start. The paper’s router thresholds lose accuracy out of sample. A router can only trade accuracy for a cost saving, and the measured cost of the specialist (a daily refit) is close to the TSFM’s. Its decision drifts: 40 of 50 series change branch over a year.

title: When does a zero-shot TSFM beat a refitted specialist?
text:
Method

Pre-registered protocols (block 2, block 3), committed before the first forecast. The one deviation (a seasonal ETS reference) is labelled wherever it appears.
Leakage tests: every refit and every context ends at the cutoff; future values are corrupted in the tests to prove it. Chronos-2’s cross_learning is pinned off.
Uncertainty over origins (moving blocks of 7 days) and over countries (block 3), never over hours.
Reproducible: bit-identical forecasts run to run; CPU vs GPU within 0.016 MW.
